preamble: The palatalized alveolar fricative [sʲ] became the alveolo-palatal fricative [ɕ] in Polish: the secondary palatal articulation was integrated into the primary constriction, moving it back from the alveolar ridge to the alveolo-palatal region. The development is characteristic of Polish (spelled ś or si); neighbouring Slavic languages diverge, with Russian and Belarusian keeping [sʲ] and Lower Sorbian hardening soft s. Padgett and Żygis attribute the Polish outcome to pressure for perceptual contrast within its three-way sibilant system /s ɕ ʂ/. A recent change among young speakers in central Poland moves in the opposite direction, from [ɕ] back to [sʲ].
phoneticEffects: Palatalization, Retraction, Change in Place of Articulation

examples.note: Soft s before the front vowel *ě developed into the alveolo-palatal fricative.
Word-final soft s before a front jer gives ś (Old Polish wieś, first attested in 1249).

sources: Padgett, J., & Żygis, M. (2007). The evolution of sibilants in Polish and Russian. Journal of Slavic Linguistics 15(2), 291–324. Earlier version: ZAS Papers in Linguistics 32 (2003). https://doi.org/10.21248/zaspil.32.2003.190

Żygis, M., & Padgett, J. (2010). A perceptual study of Polish fricatives, and its implications for historical sound change. Journal of Phonetics 38(2), 207–226. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.wocn.2009.10.003
